The Hidden Battle Within Us: Purpose, Temptation, Ego and Spiritual Growth

By R.K.
Modified date: 06/10/2026
129
3 min.
Facebook
X
Pinterest
WhatsApp
    Listen to audio version of this article
    Sponsored by
    0:00 / 4:02
    Instaread

    What happens when life looks fine on the outside, but something still feels missing within?

    In this episode of Peek Inside, Arky Jones speaks with Vladimir Cirkovic about spirituality, purpose, temptation, ego and the internal struggles that shape the way people live. Vladimir describes growing up in Serbia with a strong sense that many of life’s most important questions were rarely discussed openly. Even after studying acting and experiencing moments of success, he says he continued to feel an emptiness that external achievements did not resolve.

    That sense of dissatisfaction eventually led him towards spiritual practice. For Vladimir, a personal experience while chanting before sleep became the starting point for a much deeper exploration of spirituality, meditation and self-understanding.

    Why Material Success Does Not Always Create Fulfilment

    A recurring theme in the conversation is the difference between temporary pleasure and deeper fulfilment.

    Vladimir argues that material experiences can provide happiness for a while, but that people quickly adapt. He uses simple examples such as eating chocolate or buying a car to describe how satisfaction can fade once something becomes familiar. His wider view is that people need to pay attention not only to physical and psychological life, but also to what he sees as the spiritual side of human experience.

    Arky pushes the conversation further by questioning modern consumer culture and the way attention can become captured by short-term rewards. He also asks whether society encourages people to remain focused on external achievement rather than turning inward.

    Vladimir’s response is practical rather than purely philosophical. He argues that spirituality should not be separated from ordinary life. In his view, spiritual practice is not about withdrawing from the world, but about learning how to bring greater awareness into everyday decisions, relationships and behaviour.

    Temptation, Thoughts and the Struggle With the Self

    The conversation becomes particularly interesting when Arky introduces the idea of “demons” as a metaphor for temptation, crossroads and choices that may feel rewarding in the short term but carry consequences later.

    Vladimir expands on this by discussing anger, fear, jealousy, attachment and desire as internal weaknesses that can influence behaviour. He says the first step is recognising them before they build momentum. His description is almost psychological: a few thoughts can become repeated thoughts, then emotion, and eventually action if they are not noticed early enough.

    Arky challenges this slightly by arguing that thoughts themselves do not necessarily have power until they are acted upon. Vladimir broadly agrees, while adding that actions often begin with internal patterns that develop beforehand.

    That leads to one of the strongest ideas in the episode: Vladimir’s suggestion that people should “turn the camera inside”. He argues that individuals often assume they understand themselves better than they actually do, and that self-observation can reveal both strengths and uncomfortable weaknesses.

    Ego, Perseverance and Staying Grounded

    Later in the episode, the discussion turns to perseverance and ego.

    Vladimir says meaningful change requires consistency. Whether someone is trying to improve physically, psychologically or spiritually, he believes progress depends on continuing even when motivation fades. He also argues that change often begins internally before becoming visible in habits, relationships and life choices.

    Arky then raises a harder question: what happens when someone becomes a teacher, mentor or leader and begins to enjoy the power that comes with being listened to?

    Vladimir describes “spiritual ego” as a real danger. His way of guarding against it is to see himself as a student rather than an authority figure. He says he prefers to share rather than command, and to treat people as fellow travellers rather than followers.

    The episode ultimately becomes less about finding a single spiritual answer and more about learning how to examine yourself honestly. Whether listeners agree with all of Vladimir Cirkovic’s spiritual beliefs or not, the conversation raises worthwhile questions about purpose, attention, temptation, ego, discipline and what it means to live deliberately.
